---
name: docs-drift-check
description: Audit a repository's documentation (README, CONTRIBUTING, docs folder) against the actual code and list every statement that is no longer true, with file-and-line evidence. Use when asked to check, audit or verify docs for drift or outdated content.
---

# DocDrift: documentation drift audit

Goal: find every place where the documentation says something the code no longer supports,
prove it with evidence, and write one clear report.

Keep costs low. Do not re-read files you have already read. Use read-only `explore`
subagents for checking (they run on a lighter model and cannot change files).

<Steps>
<Step>
**Find the docs.** List the documentation files to audit, in this order:
README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, any other top-level .md files, then the docs/ folder.
If the user named specific files, audit only those. Skip CHANGELOG, LICENSE and
auto-generated API reference files. Also skip vendored and dependency folders
(node_modules, vendor, bin, obj, dist, build, .git).
</Step>

<Step>
**Extract claims.** Read the docs and pull out every statement that can be checked
against the code. Sort each one into a category from `categories.md`:
COMMAND, PATH, ENV, API, VERSION, DEPENDENCY, COUNT.
Give each claim an ID (C1, C2, ...) and record the doc file and line it came from.
Ignore opinions, marketing text and things that cannot be checked from the repo.
Write the claim list into your todo list so progress is visible.
</Step>

<Step>
**Check claims in parallel.** Spawn one read-only `explore` subagent per category
that has claims (up to six). Give each subagent:
- the list of claims in its category (ID, exact quoted text, doc location), and
- the checking rules for that category from `categories.md`.

Each subagent must return, for every claim, one verdict:
- OK: the code confirms it (cite file:line),
- DRIFT: the code contradicts it (cite file:line and say what the truth is),
- UNVERIFIED: no clear evidence either way (say what was searched).

If there are fewer than 5 claims in total, check them directly instead of spawning subagents.
</Step>

<Step>
**Double-check every DRIFT.** Before reporting a DRIFT, re-open the cited evidence
yourself and confirm it. If the evidence is weak, downgrade it to UNVERIFIED.
A false alarm is worse than a missed problem, because it destroys trust in the report.
</Step>

<Step>
**Group by root cause.** If several DRIFT claims come from the same underlying problem
(for example a missing file that is mentioned in two places), report them as ONE finding
and list all the affected claim IDs and doc lines in it. Each claim still counts
separately in the trust score.

**Rate severity** for each DRIFT using `categories.md`:
HIGH (a new developer following the docs will fail), MEDIUM (confusing or misleading),
LOW (cosmetic or minor).
</Step>

<Step>
**Write the report** to `DRIFT_REPORT.md` in the repo root, using exactly the layout in
`report-template.md`. Calculate the trust score as:
OK claims / (OK + DRIFT claims) x 100, rounded to a whole number.
UNVERIFIED claims are listed but not counted in the score.
</Step>

<Step>
**Finish** with a short chat summary: number of claims checked, number of DRIFT
findings by severity, and the trust score. Suggest switching to the Docs Fixer mode
to apply the fixes.
</Step>
</Steps>

1 | # Time Series Forecasting: LSTM vs Prophet vs ARIMA
2 | 
3 | Trains and compares three forecasting models on any stock ticker, serves predictions through a
4 | REST API, and presents everything in an interactive dashboard.
5 | 
6 | Pick a ticker and a date range, train all three models on it, then compare how they actually
7 | performed on data none of them saw during training.
8 | 
9 | ---
10 | 
11 | ## What it does
12 | 
13 | - **Fetches live data** from Yahoo Finance for any ticker, over any date range up to 5 years
14 | - **Trains three models** on the same data: a PyTorch LSTM, Facebook Prophet, and ARIMA
15 | - **Backtests them** against a held-out test period and records the results
16 | - **Serves forecasts** through a FastAPI REST API, including an ensemble that averages all three
17 | - **Versions every training run**, so retraining on 2 years vs 5 years of data produces two
18 |   separately comparable models rather than one overwriting the other
19 | 
20 | ---
21 | 
22 | ## Quick start
23 | 
24 | ### Option A: Docker (recommended)
25 | 
26 | Runs the API, dashboard, and a PostgreSQL database together, with no local Python setup at all.
27 | 
28 | ```bash
29 | docker compose up --build
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | Then open:
33 | - Dashboard: http://localhost:8501
34 | - API docs: http://localhost:8000/docs
35 | 
36 | The first build takes several minutes - PyTorch and Prophet are large. Later starts are fast.
37 | 
38 | ### Option B: Running locally
39 | 
40 | ```bash
41 | python -m venv venv
42 | venv\Scripts\activate        # Windows
43 | # source venv/bin/activate   # macOS / Linux
44 | 
45 | pip install -r requirements.txt
46 | 
47 | copy .env.example .env       # Windows
48 | # cp .env.example .env       # macOS / Linux
49 | ```
50 | 
51 | The default `.env` uses SQLite, so no database server is needed. Then, in two terminals:
52 | 
53 | ```bash
54 | uvicorn src.api.main:app --reload      # terminal 1
55 | streamlit run dashboard/app.py          # terminal 2
56 | ```
57 | 
58 | ---
59 | 
60 | ## Using it
61 | 
62 | 1. Open the dashboard and enter a ticker (e.g. `AAPL`)
63 | 2. Click **Train** in the sidebar - this trains all three models and takes a minute or two
64 | 3. Once training finishes, the **Forecasts** and **Comparison** tabs become available
65 | 
66 | The Forecasts tab plots the prediction against what actually happened. This works because
67 | forecasts begin at the model's training cutoff rather than today, so real prices usually already
68 | exist for part of the forecast window - making it a real accuracy check, not just a projection.
69 | 
70 | Nothing is pre-trained: a ticker must be trained before it can be forecast. `GET /tickers` lists
71 | which ones are ready.
72 | 
73 | ---
74 | 
75 | ## API endpoints
76 | 
77 | | Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
78 | |---|---|---|
79 | | GET | `/health` | API status, database connectivity, trained tickers |
80 | | GET | `/tickers` | Which tickers have a trained model ready |
81 | | GET | `/historical?ticker=AAPL&days=365` | Real price history |
82 | | POST | `/retrain` | Start training a ticker (returns immediately with a job id) |
83 | | GET | `/retrain-status/{job_id}` | Check on a training job |
84 | | POST | `/forecast` | Get predictions (`lstm`, `prophet`, `arima`, or `ensemble`) |
85 | | GET | `/model-comparison?ticker=AAPL` | Each model's accuracy from its last training run |
86 | 
87 | Interactive docs at http://localhost:8000/docs once the API is running.
88 | 
89 | **Training is asynchronous.** `POST /retrain` returns a `job_id` right away rather than blocking
90 | for the minutes training takes; poll `/retrain-status/{job_id}` until it reports `completed` or
91 | `failed`.
92 | 
93 | ---
94 | 
95 | ## Project structure
96 | 
97 | ```
98 | src/
99 |   config.py              All settings and limits in one place
100 |   database.py            SQLAlchemy engine and session setup
101 |   models.py              Database tables (training jobs, metrics, cached prices)
102 |   api/
103 |     main.py              FastAPI app and startup
104 |     routes.py            Endpoints
105 |     schemas.py           Request/response validation
106 |   training/
107 |     data_loader.py       Fetch from yfinance, clean, split
108 |     lstm_trainer.py      PyTorch LSTM
109 |     prophet_trainer.py   Facebook Prophet
110 |     arima_trainer.py     ARIMA
111 |     evaluation.py        Shared metrics, so all models are scored identically
112 |     pipeline.py          Runs all three as one atomic training job
113 |   inference/
114 |     predictor.py         Loads trained models and produces forecasts
115 | dashboard/app.py         Streamlit UI
116 | tests/                   68 tests
117 | exploration.ipynb        Data exploration and model comparison, with charts
118 | ```
119 | 
120 | ---
121 | 
122 | ## Tests
123 | 
124 | ```bash
125 | pytest                    # everything (~30 seconds)
126 | pytest -m "not slow"      # skip the model-training tests (~7 seconds)
127 | ```
128 | 
129 | Tests mock the Yahoo Finance API, so they never hit the network - fast, and they don't break
130 | tomorrow when prices change.
131 | 
132 | ---
133 | 
134 | ## Understanding the metrics
135 | 
136 | The Comparison tab and `/model-comparison` report four numbers per model, measured on the held-out
137 | test period - data none of the models saw during training.
138 | 
139 | | Metric | Units | Meaning |
140 | |---|---|---|
141 | | **MAE** | dollars | Average size of the error. MAE of 4.20 means predictions were off by about $4.20 on a typical day. |
142 | | **RMSE** | dollars | Same idea, but squares errors first, so large misses count for much more. |
143 | | **MAPE** | percent | Error as a share of the actual price. Comparable across tickers. |
144 | | **R-squared** | ratio | How much of the price movement the model explains. |
145 | 
146 | **MAE vs RMSE.** MAE treats a $10 miss as exactly twice as bad as a $5 miss. RMSE squares errors
147 | before averaging, so one big miss hurts far more than several small ones. Comparing them is
148 | informative: RMSE much higher than MAE means the model is usually close but occasionally badly
149 | wrong; RMSE close to MAE means errors are evenly sized.
150 | 
151 | **Why MAPE too.** Being $5 off matters much more on a $20 stock than a $500 one. MAPE normalizes
152 | for that, which is what makes comparing AAPL against a cheaper ticker meaningful.
153 | 
154 | **R-squared, including negatives.** 1.0 is perfect. 0 means the model does no better than simply
155 | predicting the average price. **Negative values mean it does worse than that** - which happens
156 | regularly in stock forecasting, and is worth reporting honestly rather than hiding.
157 | 
158 | Lower is better for the first three; higher is better for R-squared.
159 | 
160 | The Forecasts tab shows a second, different set of numbers: where real prices already exist for the
161 | forecast window, it scores the forecast currently on screen against them. That is a live check on
162 | this specific prediction, separate from the training-time metrics above.
163 | 
164 | ---
165 | 
166 | ## Design decisions worth knowing
167 | 
168 | **Per-ticker, versioned model storage.** Each training run saves to its own timestamped folder
169 | (`models/AAPL/2026-08-24_14-30-12/`), with a `latest.txt` pointer marking which run is live. The
170 | pointer only moves after all three models finish successfully - so a retrain that fails partway
171 | through leaves the previously working model serving predictions instead of corrupting it.
172 | 
173 | **Two views of the same data.** The LSTM trains on normalized 0-1 sequences; Prophet and ARIMA
174 | train on real dates and real prices. Prophet's seasonality detection specifically depends on real
175 | calendar dates, so normalizing everything up front would quietly undermine it. All metrics are
176 | reported in real price units so the three are directly comparable.
177 | 
178 | **Training data capped at 5 years.** Longer windows mix market conditions that are too different
179 | to be useful (a stock's behavior 15 years ago says little about tomorrow), and training time
180 | scales with data size.
181 | 
182 | **Forecast horizon capped at 60 days.** LSTM forecasts are autoregressive - each day's prediction
183 | feeds the next - so error compounds and accuracy degrades the further out you look.
184 | 
185 | **Forecasts start from the training cutoff, not today.** Every model is trained on data up to a
186 | specific date, and predictions continue from there. Retrain to move that anchor forward.
187 | 
188 | ---
189 | 
190 | ## Known limitations
191 | 
192 | - ARIMA uses a fixed `(1,1,1)` order rather than searching for the best fit, so its long-horizon
193 |   forecasts tend to flatten out. `pmdarima.auto_arima` would improve this.
194 | - LSTM training isn't seeded, so retraining the same ticker twice can produce noticeably different
195 |   results.
196 | - Old training runs accumulate on disk - there's no cleanup of superseded runs.
197 | - `/historical` re-fetches from Yahoo Finance on every call rather than reading its own cache.
198 | 
199 | ---
200 | 
201 | ## Stack

204 | Docker, pytest.

1 | # Time Series Forecasting: LSTM vs Prophet vs ARIMA
2 | 
3 | Trains and compares three forecasting models on any stock ticker, serves predictions through a
4 | REST API, and presents everything in an interactive dashboard.
5 | 
6 | Pick a ticker and a date range, train all three models on it, then compare how they actually
7 | performed on data none of them saw during training.
8 | 
9 | ---
10 | 
11 | ## What it does
12 | 
13 | - **Fetches live data** from Yahoo Finance for any ticker, over any date range up to 5 years
14 | - **Trains three models** on the same data: a PyTorch LSTM, Facebook Prophet, and ARIMA
15 | - **Backtests them** against a held-out test period and records the results
16 | - **Serves forecasts** through a FastAPI REST API, including an ensemble that averages all three
17 | - **Versions every training run**, so retraining on 2 years vs 5 years of data produces two
18 |   separately comparable models rather than one overwriting the other
19 | 
20 | ---
21 | 
22 | ## Quick start
23 | 
24 | ### Option A: Docker (recommended)
25 | 
26 | Runs the API, dashboard, and a PostgreSQL database together, with no local Python setup at all.
27 | 
28 | ```bash
29 | docker compose up --build
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | Then open:
33 | - Dashboard: http://localhost:8501
34 | - API docs: http://localhost:8000/docs
35 | 
36 | The first build takes several minutes - PyTorch and Prophet are large. Later starts are fast.
37 | 
38 | ### Option B: Running locally
39 | 
40 | ```bash
41 | python -m venv venv
42 | venv\Scripts\activate        # Windows
43 | # source venv/bin/activate   # macOS / Linux
44 | 
45 | pip install -r requirements.txt
46 | 
47 | copy .env.example .env       # Windows
48 | # cp .env.example .env       # macOS / Linux
49 | ```
50 | 
51 | The default `.env` uses SQLite, so no database server is needed. Then, in two terminals:
52 | 
53 | ```bash
54 | uvicorn src.api.main:app --reload      # terminal 1
55 | streamlit run dashboard/app.py          # terminal 2
56 | ```
57 | 
58 | ---
59 | 
60 | ## Using it
61 | 
62 | 1. Open the dashboard and enter a ticker (e.g. `AAPL`)
63 | 2. Click **Train** in the sidebar - this trains all three models and takes a minute or two
64 | 3. Once training finishes, the **Forecasts** and **Comparison** tabs become available
65 | 
66 | The Forecasts tab plots the prediction against what actually happened. This works because
67 | forecasts begin at the model's training cutoff rather than today, so real prices usually already
68 | exist for part of the forecast window - making it a real accuracy check, not just a projection.
69 | 
70 | Nothing is pre-trained: a ticker must be trained before it can be forecast. `GET /tickers` lists
71 | which ones are ready.
72 | 
73 | ---
74 | 
75 | ## API endpoints
76 | 
77 | | Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
78 | |---|---|---|
79 | | GET | `/health` | API status, database connectivity, trained tickers |
80 | | GET | `/tickers` | Which tickers have a trained model ready |
81 | | GET | `/historical?ticker=AAPL&days=365` | Real price history |
82 | | POST | `/retrain` | Start training a ticker (returns immediately with a job id) |
83 | | GET | `/retrain-status/{job_id}` | Check on a training job |
84 | | POST | `/forecast` | Get predictions (`lstm`, `prophet`, `arima`, or `ensemble`) |
85 | | GET | `/model-comparison?ticker=AAPL` | Each model's accuracy from its last training run |
86 | 
87 | Interactive docs at http://localhost:8000/docs once the API is running.
88 | 
89 | **Training is asynchronous.** `POST /retrain` returns a `job_id` right away rather than blocking
90 | for the minutes training takes; poll `/retrain-status/{job_id}` until it reports `completed` or
91 | `failed`.
92 | 
93 | ---
94 | 
95 | ## Project structure
96 | 
97 | ```
98 | src/
99 |   config.py              All settings and limits in one place
100 |   database.py            SQLAlchemy engine and session setup
101 |   models.py              Database tables (training jobs, metrics, cached prices)
102 |   api/
103 |     main.py              FastAPI app and startup
104 |     routes.py            Endpoints
105 |     schemas.py           Request/response validation
106 |   training/
107 |     data_loader.py       Fetch from yfinance, clean, split
108 |     lstm_trainer.py      PyTorch LSTM
109 |     prophet_trainer.py   Facebook Prophet
110 |     arima_trainer.py     ARIMA
111 |     evaluation.py        Shared metrics, so all models are scored identically
112 |     pipeline.py          Runs all three as one atomic training job
113 |   inference/
114 |     predictor.py         Loads trained models and produces forecasts
115 | dashboard/app.py         Streamlit UI
116 | tests/                   68 tests
117 | exploration.ipynb        Data exploration and model comparison, with charts
118 | ```
119 | 
120 | ---
121 | 
122 | ## Tests
123 | 
124 | ```bash
125 | pytest                    # everything (~30 seconds)
126 | pytest -m "not slow"      # skip the model-training tests (~7 seconds)
127 | ```
128 | 
129 | Tests mock the Yahoo Finance API, so they never hit the network - fast, and they don't break
130 | tomorrow when prices change.
131 | 
132 | ---
133 | 
134 | ## Understanding the metrics
135 | 
136 | The Comparison tab and `/model-comparison` report four numbers per model, measured on the held-out
137 | test period - data none of the models saw during training.
138 | 
139 | | Metric | Units | Meaning |
140 | |---|---|---|
141 | | **MAE** | dollars | Average size of the error. MAE of 4.20 means predictions were off by about $4.20 on a typical day. |
142 | | **RMSE** | dollars | Same idea, but squares errors first, so large misses count for much more. |
143 | | **MAPE** | percent | Error as a share of the actual price. Comparable across tickers. |
144 | | **R-squared** | ratio | How much of the price movement the model explains. |
145 | 
146 | **MAE vs RMSE.** MAE treats a $10 miss as exactly twice as bad as a $5 miss. RMSE squares errors
147 | before averaging, so one big miss hurts far more than several small ones. Comparing them is
148 | informative: RMSE much higher than MAE means the model is usually close but occasionally badly
149 | wrong; RMSE close to MAE means errors are evenly sized.
150 | 
151 | **Why MAPE too.** Being $5 off matters much more on a $20 stock than a $500 one. MAPE normalizes
152 | for that, which is what makes comparing AAPL against a cheaper ticker meaningful.
153 | 
154 | **R-squared, including negatives.** 1.0 is perfect. 0 means the model does no better than simply
155 | predicting the average price. **Negative values mean it does worse than that** - which happens
156 | regularly in stock forecasting, and is worth reporting honestly rather than hiding.
157 | 
158 | Lower is better for the first three; higher is better for R-squared.
159 | 
160 | The Forecasts tab shows a second, different set of numbers: where real prices already exist for the
161 | forecast window, it scores the forecast currently on screen against them. That is a live check on
162 | this specific prediction, separate from the training-time metrics above.
163 | 
164 | ---
165 | 
166 | ## Design decisions worth knowing
167 | 
168 | **Per-ticker, versioned model storage.** Each training run saves to its own timestamped folder
169 | (`models/AAPL/2026-08-24_14-30-12/`), with a `latest.txt` pointer marking which run is live. The
170 | pointer only moves after all three models finish successfully - so a retrain that fails partway
171 | through leaves the previously working model serving predictions instead of corrupting it.
172 | 
173 | **Two views of the same data.** The LSTM trains on normalized 0-1 sequences; Prophet and ARIMA
174 | train on real dates and real prices. Prophet's seasonality detection specifically depends on real
175 | calendar dates, so normalizing everything up front would quietly undermine it. All metrics are
176 | reported in real price units so the three are directly comparable.
177 | 
178 | **Training data capped at 5 years.** Longer windows mix market conditions that are too different
179 | to be useful (a stock's behavior 15 years ago says little about tomorrow), and training time
180 | scales with data size.
181 | 
182 | **Forecast horizon capped at 60 days.** LSTM forecasts are autoregressive - each day's prediction
183 | feeds the next - so error compounds and accuracy degrades the further out you look.
184 | 
185 | **Forecasts start from the training cutoff, not today.** Every model is trained on data up to a
186 | specific date, and predictions continue from there. Retrain to move that anchor forward.
187 | 
188 | ---
189 | 
190 | ## Known limitations
191 | 
192 | - ARIMA uses a fixed `(1,1,1)` order rather than searching for the best fit, so its long-horizon
193 |   forecasts tend to flatten out. `pmdarima.auto_arima` would improve this.
194 | - LSTM training isn't seeded, so retraining the same ticker twice can produce noticeably different
195 |   results.
196 | - Old training runs accumulate on disk - there's no cleanup of superseded runs.
197 | - `/historical` re-fetches from Yahoo Finance on every call rather than reading its own cache.
198 | 
199 | ---
200 | 
201 | ## Stack
202 | 
203 | Python 3.12, FastAPI, PyTorch, Prophet, statsmodels, SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, Streamlit, Plotly,
204 | Docker, pytest.

126 | def _forecast_lstm(bundle: dict, horizon_days: int) -> list:
127 |     """
128 |     The LSTM was only ever trained to do ONE thing: given `lookback` days
129 |     of prices, predict the single next day. It has no built-in way to
130 |     predict a week ahead directly.
131 | 
132 |     So to get multiple days out, we do something called an autoregressive
133 |     rollout:
134 |       1. Feed in the last known real prices, predict day 1.
135 |       2. Pretend day 1's prediction was real, add it to the window, drop
136 |          the oldest day, predict day 2 from that.
137 |       3. Repeat until we have `horizon_days` predictions.
138 | 
139 |     The catch: from step 2 onward, the model is partly predicting from its
140 |     OWN earlier guesses instead of real data. Small errors on day 1 can
141 |     nudge day 2, which nudges day 3, and so on - so accuracy typically
142 |     gets worse the further into the horizon you go. Day 1 of any LSTM
143 |     forecast is much more trustworthy than day 7.
144 |     """
145 |     model = bundle["lstm"]
146 |     scaler = bundle["scaler"]
147 |     last_known = bundle["last_known"]

153 |     window = list(scaler.transform(last_known["value"].values.reshape(-1, 1)).flatten())

155 |     predictions_scaled = []

Contents of file README.md:

1 | # Time Series Forecasting: LSTM vs Prophet vs ARIMA
2 | 
3 | Trains and compares three forecasting models on any stock ticker, serves predictions through a
4 | REST API, and presents everything in an interactive dashboard.
5 | 
6 | Pick a ticker and a date range, train all three models on it, then compare how they actually
7 | performed on data none of them saw during training.
8 | 
9 | ---
10 | 
11 | ## What it does
12 | 
13 | - **Fetches live data** from Yahoo Finance for any ticker, over any date range up to 5 years
14 | - **Trains three models** on the same data: a PyTorch LSTM, Facebook Prophet, and ARIMA
15 | - **Backtests them** against a held-out test period and records the results
16 | - **Serves forecasts** through a FastAPI REST API, including an ensemble that averages all three
17 | - **Versions every training run**, so retraining on 2 years vs 5 years of data produces two
18 |   separately comparable models rather than one overwriting the other
19 | 
20 | ---
21 | 
22 | ## Quick start
23 | 
24 | ### Option A: Docker (recommended)
25 | 
26 | Runs the API, dashboard, and a PostgreSQL database together, with no local Python setup at all.
27 | 
28 | ```bash
29 | docker compose up --build
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | Then open:
33 | - Dashboard: http://localhost:8501
34 | - API docs: http://localhost:8000/docs
35 | 
36 | The first build takes several minutes - PyTorch and Prophet are large. Later starts are fast.
37 | 
38 | ### Option B: Running locally
39 | 
40 | ```bash
41 | python -m venv venv
42 | venv\Scripts\activate        # Windows
43 | # source venv/bin/activate   # macOS / Linux
44 | 
45 | pip install -r requirements.txt
46 | 
47 | copy .env.example .env       # Windows
48 | # cp .env.example .env       # macOS / Linux
49 | ```
50 | 
51 | The default `.env` uses SQLite, so no database server is needed. Then, in two terminals:
52 | 
53 | ```bash
54 | uvicorn src.api.main:app --reload      # terminal 1
55 | streamlit run dashboard/app.py          # terminal 2
56 | ```
57 | 
58 | ---
59 | 
60 | ## Using it
61 | 
62 | 1. Open the dashboard and enter a ticker (e.g. `AAPL`)
63 | 2. Click **Train** in the sidebar - this trains all three models and takes a minute or two
64 | 3. Once training finishes, the **Forecasts** and **Comparison** tabs become available
65 | 
66 | The Forecasts tab plots the prediction against what actually happened. This works because
67 | forecasts begin at the model's training cutoff rather than today, so real prices usually already
68 | exist for part of the forecast window - making it a real accuracy check, not just a projection.
69 | 
70 | Nothing is pre-trained: a ticker must be trained before it can be forecast. `GET /tickers` lists
71 | which ones are ready.
72 | 
73 | ---
74 | 
75 | ## API endpoints
76 | 
77 | | Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
78 | |---|---|---|
79 | | GET | `/health` | API status, database connectivity, trained tickers |
80 | | GET | `/tickers` | Which tickers have a trained model ready |
81 | | GET | `/historical?ticker=AAPL&days=365` | Real price history |
82 | | POST | `/retrain` | Start training a ticker (returns immediately with a job id) |
83 | | GET | `/retrain-status/{job_id}` | Check on a training job |
84 | | POST | `/forecast` | Get predictions (`lstm`, `prophet`, `arima`, or `ensemble`) |
85 | | GET | `/model-comparison?ticker=AAPL` | Each model's accuracy from its last training run |
86 | 
87 | Interactive docs at http://localhost:8000/docs once the API is running.
88 | 
89 | **Training is asynchronous.** `POST /retrain` returns a `job_id` right away rather than blocking
90 | for the minutes training takes; poll `/retrain-status/{job_id}` until it reports `completed` or
91 | `failed`.
92 | 
93 | ---
94 | 
95 | ## Project structure
96 | 
97 | ```
98 | src/
99 |   config.py              All settings and limits in one place
100 |   database.py            SQLAlchemy engine and session setup
101 |   models.py              Database tables (training jobs, metrics, cached prices)
102 |   api/
103 |     main.py              FastAPI app and startup
104 |     routes.py            Endpoints
105 |     schemas.py           Request/response validation
106 |   training/
107 |     data_loader.py       Fetch from yfinance, clean, split
108 |     lstm_trainer.py      PyTorch LSTM
109 |     prophet_trainer.py   Facebook Prophet
110 |     arima_trainer.py     ARIMA
111 |     evaluation.py        Shared metrics, so all models are scored identically
112 |     pipeline.py          Runs all three as one atomic training job
113 |   inference/
114 |     predictor.py         Loads trained models and produces forecasts
115 | dashboard/app.py         Streamlit UI
116 | tests/                   68 tests
117 | exploration.ipynb        Data exploration and model comparison, with charts
118 | ```
119 | 
120 | ---
121 | 
122 | ## Tests
123 | 
124 | ```bash
125 | pytest                    # everything (~30 seconds)
126 | pytest -m "not slow"      # skip the model-training tests (~7 seconds)
127 | ```
128 | 
129 | Tests mock the Yahoo Finance API, so they never hit the network - fast, and they don't break
130 | tomorrow when prices change.
131 | 
132 | ---
133 | 
134 | ## Understanding the metrics
135 | 
136 | The Comparison tab and `/model-comparison` report four numbers per model, measured on the held-out
137 | test period - data none of the models saw during training.
138 | 
139 | | Metric | Units | Meaning |
140 | |---|---|---|
141 | | **MAE** | dollars | Average size of the error. MAE of 4.20 means predictions were off by about $4.20 on a typical day. |
142 | | **RMSE** | dollars | Same idea, but squares errors first, so large misses count for much more. |
143 | | **MAPE** | percent | Error as a share of the actual price. Comparable across tickers. |
144 | | **R-squared** | ratio | How much of the price movement the model explains. |
145 | 
146 | **MAE vs RMSE.** MAE treats a $10 miss as exactly twice as bad as a $5 miss. RMSE squares errors
147 | before averaging, so one big miss hurts far more than several small ones. Comparing them is
148 | informative: RMSE much higher than MAE means the model is usually close but occasionally badly
149 | wrong; RMSE close to MAE means errors are evenly sized.
